reviews.title: A Calm and Unique Journey That Won’t Be for Everyone
reviews.text:
I had a good experience with Naiad, but it’s definitely a very specific type of game.

Movement feels smooth overall, and there are a few different ways to swim which keeps it interesting. One thing I didn’t enjoy as much was moving through polluted water it slows you down a lot. It makes sense for the game’s environmental theme, but it can feel a bit frustrating.

Interacting with the environment is enjoyable, but it can become a bit repetitive over time. Some interactions feel like variations of things you’ve already done rather than completely new ideas.

Some areas of the game can feel quite small unless you take the time to explore. It’s very easy to swim past secrets and miss content, so it’s worth slowing down and paying attention.

The art style fits the game really well. It’s simple and clean, and it works nicely with the calm and relaxing atmosphere.

For me, the game felt slightly too long for what it offers, although that will depend on how thoroughly you explore. It still feels like a complete experience overall.

I didn’t run into any technical issues during my playthrough.

Overall, I would recommend it, but mainly for players who enjoy slower, more relaxing exploration games. It’s not very challenging, but it’s unique and atmospheric.

reviews.title: A Strong Sequel That Leans More Into Combat
reviews.text:
If you enjoyed Figment, then Figment 2: Creed Valley is definitely worth playing.

Combat feels smoother and more polished compared to the first game. There’s a good variety of enemies, although I did find some frustration with certain ones like the slammer, which could be hard to target and damage. Boss fights were a highlight, especially the final musical one.

The puzzles are creative and I liked the open-/closed-minded mechanic that changes how the environment works. But the game feels a bit more combat-focused rather than puzzles like the first one.

The music and sound design are great and play a big role in the overall experience. The soundtrack really enhances the game, especially during key moments.

Visually, the game looks great. The surreal mind-world style is varied and interesting throughout. One downside for me was that the game is quite linear and doesn’t allow backtracking, which I missed from the first game.

The story was enjoyable and had a nice twist on expectations, showing that what seems like the “villain” might not actually be one.

The game is a bit longer than the first, but it doesn’t feel too long.

I did run into a couple of softlocks where I couldn’t progress. Restarting the chapter fixed it without losing much progress, but it was still a bit annoying.

Overall, a solid sequel that improves on the original in many ways. Recommended, especially if you liked the first game.

reviews.title: Roll, Upgrade, Repeat, A Short but Satisfying Loop
reviews.text:
Incredicer is a simple but satisfying incremental dice game.

The core gameplay loop of rolling dice, earning money, and buying upgrades works well. Progression feels balanced for most of the game, although it slows down quite a bit toward the end.

Upgrades mostly increase numbers or add small modifiers. They work, but I would’ve liked more noticeable feedback when they trigger. A lot of the time it just feels like numbers going up rather than meaningful changes to gameplay and visuals

The helper hands take a while to feel useful. Early on it’s faster to just roll manually, but later they become more relevant. Idle mode pushes the game even further into automation making it feel less like an incremental game and while it’s optional, once it’s there you’ll probably use it.

There’s no prestige system like in many other incremental games, so it’s just one continuous run. For a short game that works fine, but it does limit replayability.

The UI is clean and easy to understand, although a bit basic visually. Endgame becomes very cluttered to the point where you can barely see your screen.

Overall, if you enjoy incremental games and want something short and inexpensive, this is worth picking up.

reviews.title: A Relaxing and Rewarding Exploration Journey
reviews.text:
Caravan SandWitch is a really enjoyable exploration-focused game with a relaxing atmosphere.

Driving around in the van feels great, and I liked how it’s not just used for transportation but also as a tool to interact with the world. The game encourages exploration by letting you revisit areas as you unlock new mechanics that open up new paths and sections.

Progression kept me engaged the whole way through. Between resource gathering, daily missions, exploration, and story elements, there was always something to work towards. The game also does a great job guiding you with logs, markers, and clear visual and sound cues.

Visually, the game is beautiful and has a very calming atmosphere that fits the experience perfectly.

The story was interesting and well integrated into the exploration, which made everything feel more meaningful.

The length and pacing felt just right, it never felt too long or too short.

I did run into a couple of minor issues where I couldn’t interact with objects or continue dialogue and had to reload. There’s also a small frustration where if your van gets stuck, you can’t interact with anything due to overlapping keybinds, forcing you to return to the garage.

Overall, a very solid and relaxing experience that I would definitely recommend.

reviews.title: Realistic, Cinematic, and Memorable Campaign
reviews.text:
If you're looking for a cinematic and immersive FPS campaign, Call of Duty: Modern Warfare delivers.

Gunplay feels very satisfying and realistic, with a wide variety of weapons and attachments. Movement is solid overall, although the sliding mechanic feels a bit out of place, breaking the realistic feeling but not by much.

Mission variety is one of the game’s strongest aspects. There’s a great mix of environments and playstyles, with standout moments like stealth missions, house raids, and sniper sequences. The pacing between slower, tense moments and full combat works really well.

On higher difficulties, the AI can feel a bit unfair at times, but it pushes you to adapt and play more carefully.

Sound design is excellent and adds a lot to the immersion. Everything from gunfire to environmental audio feels impactful.

The story is engaging and benefits from multiple perspectives. It also tackles more serious and morally complex themes, showing that modern warfare isn’t always clear-cut.

Visually, the game looks fantastic with detailed environments and strong presentation.

The campaign length is solid, though it could have been a bit longer.

Overall I highly recommend it and if you plan to only play through the campaign I would wait for it to go on sale.

reviews.title: Satisfying Core Loop Held Back by Repetition
reviews.text:
Unboxathon is built around a simple idea to opening boxes and to its credit, it actually feels pretty satisfying at first.

The core loop is straightforward: open boxes, buy upgrades, and interact with small side mechanics like popping bubbles to earn more boxes. It works well early on and has a nice, satisfying flow, but it becomes repetitive over time.

There’s very little variety in the gameplay. Higher-tier boxes mostly just add extra straps to cut, and other mechanics feel like slight variations of the same idea rather than something new. It adds to the satisfaction a bit, but not enough to keep things feeling fresh.

Visually, the game looks good. The cute art style fits perfectly and helps make the experience more enjoyable. However the UI and menus could use some work, some features feel easy to forget about because they’re not presented clearly enough.

The length feels about right for what the game offers. Since it can get repetitive, it’s a good thing it doesn’t drag on too long.

Overall, a solid core concept that just needs more variety and depth. I’d recommend picking it up on sale rather than at full price.

reviews.title: Simple Concept, Weak Puzzle Design
reviews.text:
Access Denied is a short puzzle game where you solve 36 different mechanical boxes.

At first it’s pretty engaging, but it quickly starts to feel repetitive since many of the puzzles reuse similar ideas. The bigger issue though is the puzzle design itself. Most puzzles are either very easy or just confusing, without hitting that satisfying middle ground where solving them feels rewarding.

Visually, the game is clean and simple, which works well for this type of game. Unfortunately the sound design doesn’t hold up, audio feels a bit low quality and doesn’t add much to the experience.

The game is also very short. I finished it in under an hour, and combined with the lack of variety, it makes the experience feel quite limited.

Overall, it has a decent concept, but the execution falls short. I wouldn’t recommend it.

reviews.title: Short, Addictive, and Surprisingly Polished Incremental Fun
reviews.text:
Space Rock Breaker is a really satisfying incremental game with a strong gameplay loop.

You spend most of your time flying around in a spaceship breaking rocks to collect ore, while also managing resources through a plinko-style system, opening loot boxes, and upgrading your ship. The game constantly feeds progression, which makes it fun the entire time.

Upgrades feel meaningful and well balanced, and you can clearly feel your power increasing. There is a prestige system, but it felt a bit unnecessary since I was able to finish the game without really needing to use it more than once.

The visuals have a nice old-school CRT style that fits the game well and keeps everything looking clean.

The game is quite short, and there isn’t much reason to keep playing after beating it, but it doesn’t overstay its welcome.

Overall, a well-made incremental game that I’d recommend if you enjoy this type of experience.

reviews.title: Fun at First, But Quickly Turns Into Idle Chaos
reviews.text:
Rocket Rats is a fun survivor-like game that starts strong but becomes repetitive fairly quickly.

At the beginning, the gameplay feels engaging and rewarding. There’s a good variety of weapons, abilities, and characters, each with their own skill trees, which makes experimenting with builds enjoyable.

However, once you get stronger and figure out the optimal upgrades, the game shifts into a much more passive experience. It often feels like you’re just standing still, picking upgrades, and watching enemies die, which takes away from the initial excitement.

The art style is a highlight. The cute and polished pixel visuals fit the game really well and give it a nice charm.

One thing that didn’t fully work for me was the very small play area combined with quite intense screen shake, which can feel a bit overwhelming during gameplay.

The game is fairly short if you’re not going for 100%, but there is some replay value if you enjoy trying different builds.

On the positive side, the experience was very smooth overall. I didn’t encounter any bugs or technical issues during my playthrough.

If you enjoy survivor-like games, this is worth checking out but I’d recommend waiting for a sale rather than paying full price.

reviews.title: A Slower, Less Impactful Follow-Up
reviews.text:
It didn’t leave a great first impression. I actually ended up enjoying it more on a second playthrough while going for achievements, which isn’t the best sign. If I wasn’t committed to finishing it, I probably wouldn’t have played as much.

Controlling the ship and submarine feels smooth, and managing the different systems can be engaging. That said, moving around inside the ship can be awkward, and I found myself falling between levels or missing jumps more than I expected.

The biggest issue for me is the pacing. There are long sailing sections where you don’t really have to do anything, and those moments felt more slow than relaxing.

The puzzles are a mix of simple and interesting ideas, and they fit well into the world, but I felt like there were too few of them.

Atmosphere is still strong. The world feels immersive and the sound design does a good job supporting it. Visually it’s more colorful than the first game, but somehow felt a bit less polished.

I also ran into some minor issues like animation problems and invisible platforms after moving objects.

Overall, it’s not a bad game, but compared to FAR: Lone Sails it feels like a downgrade in pacing and overall experience.

reviews.title: Charming, Creative, and Surprisingly Clever
reviews.text:
Webbed is a really fun and charming game.

The web swinging feels satisfying right away, but the web-building mechanic can be a bit frustrating at the start until you get used to it. Once it clicks though, it becomes a big part of what makes the game enjoyable, especially when solving puzzles.

The puzzles are creative and each area of the map introduces different ideas, which keeps things interesting throughout the game.

The pixel art looks great and the animations give the game a lot of charm. Overall it has a very cute style that fits the experience perfectly.

The length felt just right for me. I went for 100% completion and the collectibles were fun to get. The map clearly shows which areas still have collectibles left, which makes it much easier to clean up without it feeling tedious.

Overall, if you like platformers with creative mechanics and a charming style, this is definitely worth playing.

reviews.title: A Clever Hidden Gem with a Unique Twist
reviews.text:
Is This Game Trying to Kill Me? is a really unique puzzle game and honestly feels like a hidden gem.

The main mechanic revolves around a game-within-a-game concept where you interact with both the cabin environment and a retro-style game running inside it. The way these two layers connect is very well executed and makes the puzzles feel creative and different from most puzzle games.

The puzzles themselves were great. They’re clever, varied, and fun to solve. The logic behind them always felt fair, and I never had to rely on random trial and error to progress.

The game has some horror vibes and elements, but it’s much more puzzle-focused than scary, which I personally liked.

I also enjoyed the contrast between the visual styles. The cabin setting combined with the retro game aesthetic works really well and helps sell the whole concept.

Technically the game ran very smoothly for me and I didn’t encounter any bugs or issues during my playthrough.

Overall, if you enjoy puzzle games with clever mechanics and fair puzzle design, this one is definitely worth playing.

reviews.title: A Calm but Slightly Repetitive Dive into a Strong Story
reviews.text:
I finished Under the Waves and I had a good experience with it.

The game recommends playing with a controller, but I used keyboard and mouse. Movement felt mostly fine for me. It can feel a little clunky from time to time, but it wasn’t a major issue.

Exploration works well for the type of game this is. Since the focus is on story and atmosphere, moving through the underwater environments feels relaxing and fits the tone of the game nicely.

The gameplay loop involves exploring, gathering resources, crafting, and maintaining equipment. Because the game isn’t very long, the loop stays fairly engaging. That said, I felt there was slightly too much gathering and crafting. I ended up collecting a lot of resources that I rarely needed to use, so sometimes it felt like filler just to give the player something to do between story sections. This also meant getting in and out of the submarine quite often, which became a bit repetitive.

The story itself is very good. It’s emotional and impactful, and it’s clearly the main focus of the experience.

The atmosphere is another highlight. The sound design, ocean environments, and overall feeling of isolation are very well done. The map size feels appropriate, and there are some nice touches like cinematic camera shots, the ability to toggle the HUD for immersion, and small interaction details. The marine life also adds a lot to the world.

The only technical issue I ran into was with animations occasionally being slightly off or not fully synced with the interaction happening on screen. It didn’t break anything, but it was noticeable a few times.

Overall, Under the Waves is a strong narrative and atmospheric experience. If you enjoy slower-paced story-driven games with exploration, it’s definitely worth playing.

reviews.title: A Short, Charming, and Silly Stretchy Adventure
reviews.text:
Completely Stretchy is a fun and silly little game.

The stretchy arm mechanic feels great once you get used to it. It takes a bit of practice at first, but the movement becomes very smooth once you understand how to use the momentum while swinging around the environment.

The puzzles and quests are generally simple but they’re varied enough that the game rarely feels repetitive.

Exploring the three islands was enjoyable. Each one has a different theme, city, industrial, and nature and the world never really felt empty. There are always strange characters around doing random things, which adds a lot of charm.

I liked the colorful cartoon style overall, although some areas felt a little bland because of the heavy use of solid colors and minimal textures.

The length felt right for this kind of game. It’s short but doesn’t feel rushed. Going for all achievements was mostly enjoyable, although the collectible cleanup near the end became a bit tedious.

I did encounter a few bugs during my playthrough. Some achievements didn’t trigger properly, and I got stuck in the environment a few times. Reloading the save fixed those situations, but one achievement bug required starting a new save to complete it. Luckily it could be completed at the beginning of the game.

Overall it’s a short, charming, and slightly weird experience. If you want to try something different and lighthearted, it’s definitely worth checking out.

reviews.title: A Stylish Western Shooter That Hits More Than It Misses
reviews.text:
Call of Juarez: Gunslinger was a really enjoyable experience.

The gunplay feels clean and satisfying. Combat is fast and arcade-like, which fits the game well. The only gameplay issue I noticed was that occasionally when aiming directly at an enemy and shooting, the hit wouldn’t register. It didn’t happen constantly, but it was noticeable when it did.

The duel mechanic was a highlight. It takes a bit of practice to understand how it works, but once it clicks it becomes very fun. The game also adds new elements to duels later in the story, like dodging and switching targets, which keeps them interesting. I did encounter a small bug a couple of times where the duel animation delayed, I heard the gunshot and died before the character even reached for his gun. Reloading the checkpoint fixed it.

The skill tree is decent. Some skills noticeably improve gameplay while others are smaller upgrades, but that works fine for the type of shooter this is.

I usually don’t prioritize story in games, but the way it’s presented here is very entertaining. The whole game is Silas Greene telling his story in a saloon, and the world literally changes as he corrects or exaggerates parts of the story. That mechanic alone makes the game stand out.

The art style also holds up well. The comic-book look gives it a bit of a cel-shaded feel similar to Borderlands, and it still looks good today. The cinematic moments where the action freezes into comic-book style panels are a nice touch too and reinforce the game’s identity.

Difficulty scaling felt fair overall. Higher difficulties were challenging but manageable. The only downside is that the hardest difficulty is locked until you beat the previous one, which I’m personally not a fan of.

The campaign itself is fairly short, but if you’re going for achievements or 100% completion there’s still a decent amount of content. The arcade and duels mode add some extra challenges.

Overall, a very fun and stylish western shooter that doesn’t overstay its welcome.

reviews.title: Creative, Clever, and Worth Experiencing
reviews.text:
Hello, my name is Dr. Glenn Pierce.

I really enjoyed Superliminal.

The perspective-based resizing mechanic is the highlight. It’s simple to understand but clever in execution. The game doesn’t over-explain anything, you pick up an object in the first room, experiment for a few seconds, and immediately understand how it works.

The puzzles aren’t extremely difficult, but they make you think just enough. For me, the difficulty scaled properly and the solutions felt intuitive. I rarely felt stuck because of unclear logic.

It’s also short and focused, which I personally see as a positive. The only real downside is that it might feel slightly overpriced for the length. That said, there are community-made levels if you want more content.

I enjoyed the narrative tone as well. It gave off strong Stanley Parable vibes with its calm, slightly surreal presentation.

Replayability was surprisingly solid too. I had a lot of fun going for all achievements and learning speedrun strategies. The mechanics hold up well when you start optimizing movement and puzzle execution.

Overall, if you like creative puzzle games with a unique core mechanic and a focused runtime, this is definitely worth playing.

reviews.title: Great Story, Frustrating Gameplay
reviews.text:
Spec Ops: The Line is praised heavily for its story, and I agree that the narrative is the strongest part of the game. It’s uncomfortable, memorable, and clearly the focus.

But for me, gameplay matters more than narrative and that’s where the experience fell apart.

If you just want to experience the story, play on Easy or Normal. You’ll probably have a much better time.

I played on higher difficulties because I enjoy a challenge and wanted to 100% the game. The hardest difficulty is locked until you beat the game on the second hardest, which already felt unnecessary. If I want to start on the hardest mode, let me.

And every time you boot the game it checks for updates before even entering the campaign, that could easily be triggered when entering multiplayer instead.

On higher difficulty the problems become very noticeable:

- The game constantly asks if you want to lower the difficulty after repeated deaths.
- Some checkpoints are placed before cutscenes, forcing you to rewatch them after dying (not all are skippable).
- The camera can be blocked by the environment, and sometimes your own character gets in the way of your aim.
- Sprinting lowers turning sensitivity so much that quick adjustments are difficult and also sprinting isn’t always available.
- The gameplay itself is a very standard cover-based shooter.
- The AI on higher difficulty feels unfair rather than challenging — snapping to your position, extremely accurate, high damage, constant suppression, limited ammo, while your own accuracy and movement feel restricted.

The result is frustration instead of tension.

I understand why people praise the story. I just don’t think the mechanics justify a 92% positive rating, especially if you value gameplay over narrative.

If story is your priority, you may love it.
If mechanics and difficulty design matter more to you, your experience might differ.

reviews.title: Constant Progression Done Right
reviews.text:
This Ain’t Even Poker, Ya Joker is a really enjoyable incremental game with a lot more depth than it first appears.

Most of your time is spent flipping cards, earning money, expanding your deck, and buying upgrades. It’s satisfying and fun, with a steady stream of things to manage and improve. It gets a little repetitive toward the very end, but the game finishes at about the right time.

What really kept me engaged was how many mechanics the game introduces over time. Expeditions, Joker cards, quests, prestige upgrades, and rune crafting all add meaningful progression. Everything scales well and there’s almost always something to do, so it rarely feels idle.

Visually, I liked the top-down perspective in a 3D environment, and I appreciated that many interactable elements actually contribute to gameplay.

Sound effects are satisfying, although things can get a bit overwhelming once the game becomes chaotic.

No technical issues during my playthrough, it felt polished throughout.

Overall, definitely recommended, especially if you’re a fan of incremental games.

reviews.title: Decent Core Ideas, But Far Too Barebones
reviews.text:
I wanted to like Goobies more than I did, but it feels too barebones right now.

The gameplay is smooth for the most part, though the momentum-based character felt awkward to use. The bigger issue is repetition. Maps and enemies are extremely basic, and since runs are endless, there’s no satisfying conclusion to them. After a few runs, it all starts to feel the same.

There is some build variety, and I liked how weapon upgrades evolve into stronger versions with added traits instead of just boosting stats. But because everything is unlocked from the start and there’s no real limit on what you can stack, most runs ended up looking very similar anyway.

Progression feels very slow and not especially rewarding. It often didn’t feel like I was working toward anything meaningful, which is a major problem for a game built around repeated runs.

The visuals are probably the strongest part. The goofy style gives the game some charm. But once the screen fills up in the mid and late game, it becomes cluttered and hard to read, and I even had performance issues because of it.

There’s an alright core here, but it needs much more content, balance, and a better progression loop. As it stands, I can’t recommend it unless you get it free or very cheap and just want a few hours with a simple survivor-like.

reviews.title: A short and clever card-based puzzle climb
reviews.text:
Golf Peaks is a short and clever puzzle game with a strong card-based movement system.

Instead of directly controlling the ball, you use cards to decide how it moves. I liked this mechanic a lot, and it reminded me a little of Please, Fix the Road, except here you can choose the cards in any order. That gives the puzzles a nice sense of flexibility.

The game does a good job of avoiding repetition. Each world is fairly short, and new mechanics are introduced regularly. The difficulty curve also feels fair, as each new world gives you time to learn its mechanic before the puzzles become harder.

Some puzzles toward the end of certain worlds can be quite challenging, and I think a hint button would have been a nice addition. I also would have liked the option to rearrange cards in my hand, and some cards could have been more visually distinct since they can look quite similar.

The clean minimalist isometric art style fits the game very well, and the mechanics are nicely designed around the themes of each world. The soundtrack is relaxing and works for the atmosphere, although it is not especially memorable.

The game is short and sweet, which suited it well. It does not overstay its welcome, and I had no technical issues during my playthrough.

Overall, Golf Peaks is an enjoyable and well-designed puzzle game. I would recommend it, especially if you like smaller relaxing puzzle games. Pick it up on sale if you can, but the full price still feels fair.

reviews.title: A Magical and Immersive Open-World Experience
reviews.text:
Hogwarts Legacy is a great open-world game that really captures the atmosphere and feeling of the Wizarding World.

Combat was fun throughout the game. There are lots of different spells, mechanics, combos, and traits that allow you to enhance your playstyle. Enemy shields and combat feats also force you to use different spell types, which adds variety and keeps combat from becoming too repetitive.

The world feels very alive. Hogwarts, Hogsmeade, and the rest of the open world are filled with places to explore, including rooms, houses, villages, structures, dens, challenges, loot, collectibles, characters, and enemies. There is always something to find, and the environments are very detailed.

The story was engaging, even for someone like me who does not usually focus that much on story. Dialogue choices also felt somewhat meaningful, which helped make the experience more interesting.

Graphically, the game looks amazing. The music, voice acting, and overall audio design are also great and really help build the atmosphere.

The pacing was good during the main story, but after finishing it, the remaining side content became a bit too much. Challenges and collectibles started to feel repetitive, and some things were not very easy to find or keep track of.

I also ran into some technical issues. Going through doors was not always smooth, cloth physics acted up sometimes, and the final Crossed Wands round was a bit buggy and frustrating. Even on a high-end PC, I had some performance issues and had to lower my settings. I also noticed occasional Z-fighting, and lighting sometimes broke when entering houses during daytime, making interiors extremely bright.

Overall, Hogwarts Legacy is definitely worth playing. It is immersive, beautiful, and fun, with a lot of content. I would recommend it, but because of the high price, it might be worth waiting for a sale.

reviews.title: Magnetic Mechanics Done Right
reviews.text:
Mind Over Magnet is a creative puzzle platformer with a strong central mechanic that stays enjoyable throughout the entire game.

The magnet mechanics are genuinely fun to use and the game does a great job of introducing new ideas frequently enough that puzzles never really become repetitive. The levels are divided into different worlds, each with their own mechanics and twists, which keeps the experience feeling fresh.

The puzzles have a solid difficulty balance overall. Some made me stop and think for a bit, while others only took longer because of my own mistakes. I also appreciated the hint system and how naturally it’s implemented into the game.

Controls feel smooth and precise, which is important for this type of game and I never felt like I was fighting the mechanics.

Visually and audibly the game is fairly basic but still pleasant enough and fitting for the experience.

It’s a fairly short game but I think the length works well since the game introduces new mechanics at a steady pace without dragging things out.

I also had a completely smooth experience technically with no bugs or issues during my playthrough.

Overall, I’d definitely recommend it to fans of puzzle platformers and creative mechanics. The only thing holding me back slightly is the price, which feels a little high for the amount of content so I’d probably wait for a sale.

reviews.title: A Fun LEGO Adventure With Plenty to Discover
reviews.text:
LEGO Jurassic World is an enjoyable LEGO adventure that offers plenty of exploration, collectibles, and lighthearted gameplay.

The gameplay offers a nice mix of combat, exploration, puzzles, quick-time events, and open-world activities. Compared to some previous LEGO games I've played, it felt a bit different in a good way. While things became slightly repetitive towards the end, there was enough variety throughout most of the game to keep me engaged.

The character roster is one of the highlights. Many characters have multiple uses, which makes exploration and puzzle-solving more interesting. I was also pleasantly surprised that you also get to play as the dinosaurs. That being said, some of the larger dinosaurs was a bit awkward to control. One thing I struggled with throughout the game was remembering which characters could perform specific actions, and I think the game could do a better job communicating that information.

Exploration was probably my favorite part of the experience. The open-world areas are enjoyable to explore, the map is a welcome addition, and being able to select individual sections of completed levels makes collectible hunting much more manageable. Most collectibles were fun to find, although some during chase sequences were frustrating since camera angles made them difficult to spot even with the collectible detector enabled.

The environments look good and the soundtrack helps support the atmosphere. On the technical side, I encountered a couple of crashes during my playthrough. It was also fairly easy to get characters stuck in the environment, although switching characters usually fixed the issue. I also ran into some targeting frustrations and occasional animation glitches.

Overall, LEGO Jurassic World is a fun LEGO adventure with enjoyable exploration, a good amount of variety, and plenty of content for completionists. If you enjoy LEGO games, this is an easy recommendation.

reviews.title: A Brilliant Vampire Survival Experience
reviews.text:
V Rising is an outstanding survival crafting experience.

The combat feels fantastic from beginning to end. It's responsive, satisfying, and offers a huge amount of build variety through different weapons, spells, passives, and jewel modifications. Every V Blood boss feels unique and requires a different approach, making each victory rewarding. We played on Brutal difficulty, which was challenging without ever feeling unfair. Learning boss mechanics and improving over time made every encounter satisfying. It's also fun when roaming bosses unexpectedly run into each other and start fighting.

Castle building is another standout feature. The building system is intuitive and easy to use, and I really enjoyed designing, decorating, and continuously expanding my castle. New crafting stations, decorations, and upgrades keep unlocking throughout the game, giving you plenty of reasons to keep improving your base.

Exploration is consistently rewarding. Every region has its own distinct atmosphere, enemies, resources, and bosses, so there's always something new to discover.

Progression is excellent. Unlocking new abilities, crafting stations, and recipes through boss kills and research always feels meaningful. I expected the game to be much grindier than it actually was. Gathering resources can occasionally become a little repetitive, but it never felt excessive.

I had previously played the game solo and never finished it, but this time I experienced it with two friends in PvE, which made the game even more enjoyable. We skipped PvP entirely, and for us that was the right choice.

Visually, the game looks great. The gothic art style, music, and sound design all work together to create a fantastic vampire atmosphere. The gameplay is clearly the main focus rather than the story, and that's exactly where the game excels.

The game is quite long but never overstays its welcome because there's always another meaningful goal to work towards.

Performance was flawless during my playthrough. I didn't experience any bugs or technical issues.

Overall, V Rising is an outstanding survival game with excellent combat, rewarding progression, satisfying base building, and a world that's genuinely fun to explore. Highly recommended.

reviews.title: A Surprisingly Challenging Test of Finger Coordination
reviews.text:
Fingerdance is a fun and unique rhythm game that challenged my coordination far more than I expected.

The concept is simple: assign one key to each finger and hit the correct notes as they appear. It took me a while to find a comfortable keybind layout, but once I did, the controls felt responsive and satisfying. Most of the difficulty came from getting my brain and fingers to communicate properly rather than from the game itself.

The difficulty is well balanced throughout the levels. It can be challenging at times, but it always felt fair and rewarding as I improved.

The presentation is clean and minimal, which fits the game perfectly. The UI is easy to read, and the notes are clear and easy to follow.

The game is quite short, only taking a couple of hours to complete. Because of that, it never overstays its welcome or becomes repetitive. However, I don't see much replay value, and I found myself needing regular breaks since the gameplay can be surprisingly mentally demanding.

Overall, I'd recommend Fingerdance if you're looking for a short, unique rhythm game. It's a fun experience, although I think the price could be slightly lower considering the limited amount of content.

reviews.title: The house always wins... especially against your friends
reviews.text:
If you're looking for a casual party game to play with friends, Gamble With Your Friends is a solid choice.

The game offers a good variety of casino games that gradually unlock as you reach new floors. You'll find everything from slots, blackjack, roulette, crash, keno, and plinko to several other games. Each one is fun on its own, but after a while the overall gameplay loop starts to become repetitive. Most of the games are based more on luck than strategy, although a few let you make small decisions that can either save you or make you lose everything because you got a little too greedy.

I played both solo and multiplayer, and it's clear that this game is built around playing with friends. Most of my solo time was just spent cleaning up achievements. Multiplayer is where the game shines, with lots of funny interactions between players. Watching your friends lose all their money, secretly changing their bet size, or jumping into their game creates plenty of memorable moments.

The controls are responsive, the UI is straightforward, and it's very easy to understand how everything works.

The art style is simple but charming, fitting the game's goofy atmosphere well. The animations and sound effects are fairly basic, but they get the job done, and the music suits the casino setting nicely.

Run lengths can vary a lot. Sometimes you'll lose everything almost immediately simply because luck wasn't on your side. After several unlucky runs, I definitely felt less motivated to keep playing. On the bright side, there's a decent amount of content, and I think the asking price is fair for what the game offers. It also reinforces one important lesson: gamble with fake money, not real money.

I did run into a few issues. Some challenges referenced games that didn't appear on the current floors, although they still progressed on different machines. The phone in the lobby could still be answered by players joining late, rerolling challenges unexpectedly. The emote wheel occasionally selected the wrong emote, NPCs often stood in front of machines and became more annoying than immersive, and the repeated trips back to the car between days eventually felt like unnecessary downtime. The camera animation when starting a new day also became a bit hard to watch after a while, with your character getting launched out of the box over and over again.

Overall, I had a good time with Gamble With Your Friends. It probably won't keep you hooked for dozens of hours, but it's an easy game to recommend if you want a few evenings full of laughs with friends at a reasonable price.

reviews.title: A classic browser game that doesn't quite strike gold on Steam
reviews.text:
Gold Miner is one of those games that many people remember fondly, and I completely understand why. It was a fantastic browser game back in 2003, and replaying it definitely brought back some nostalgic memories.

That said, I don't think nostalgia alone should determine whether a modern Steam release is worth recommending.

The gameplay is still simple and easy to understand, but after a short while it started feeling repetitive. The Steam version adds a new game mode and a few small extra things, but overall it's still essentially the same game many of us played for free years ago. Even the menus and general presentation feel a bit rough.

If you're buying this purely to relive your childhood, you'll probably have a good time for an hour or so, just like I did. But if you've never played Gold Miner before, I don't think it holds up particularly well compared to what's available today, especially at its current price.

I respect what Gold Miner meant to gaming history, but this Steam release feels like it's relying more on nostalgia than offering enough value as a modern release.

reviews.title: Solid Foundation, But Needs More Variety
reviews.text:
Duncrush has a solid foundation, but it could use a bit more variety to stay engaging throughout.

The core gameplay loop of clearing dungeon floors, collecting loot, and becoming stronger is enjoyable at first. However, it becomes repetitive fairly quickly. While each floor introduces something new, most additions feel minor, and the enemies, equipment, and environments are largely the same with different visual themes.

I wasn't a fan of the click-to-move controls. For this type of game, keyboard movement would have felt much more natural. Combat is also quite basic, and the very short attack range often means you have to stand almost on top of enemies, trading damage rather than avoiding it.

The retro presentation is well done. The pixel art, sound effects, and soundtrack all fit the game's old-school style nicely. Nothing particularly stands out, but the overall presentation is solid.

Progression is decent, and you definitely feel stronger as you unlock better gear. I especially enjoyed unlocking companions that help you fight through the dungeons.

The game only lasts a few hours, which works in its favor since there isn't a huge amount of content. It's reasonably priced, although I'd recommend grabbing it on sale if you can.

Performance was flawless during my playthrough, and I didn't encounter any bugs or technical issues.

Overall, I still recommend Duncrush. It has a fun core gameplay loop and is an enjoyable short experience, but it would benefit from more gameplay variety and a few improvements to combat and movement.

reviews.title: A Brilliant Puzzle Game That's Just a Little Too Short
reviews.text:
Viewfinder is one of the more creative puzzle games I've played.

The photography mechanic is fantastic. Being able to place photos into the world and reshape the environment never got old, and the game does a great job introducing new mechanics throughout the adventure without making things feel repetitive.

Most puzzles are on the easier side, but they're still satisfying to solve because there are often multiple ways to approach them. I frequently questioned whether I had solved a puzzle as intended or had simply found my own solution, which made experimentation a lot of fun. The optional challenge levels offer a nice increase in difficulty for players looking for more.

The visuals are excellent and play a huge role in the experience. The environments are varied, and unlocking camera filters that change how parts of the world look is a fun addition. Combined with the relaxing soundtrack, narration, and voice acting, the game creates a very calming atmosphere.

The story is interesting enough, but it mainly serves to support the gameplay rather than being the main reason to play.

Controls are intuitive, the UI is clean, and I encountered no bugs or performance issues during my playthrough.

My only real complaint is the length and pricing. The game is fairly short, and although I finished it wanting more, I don't think it's worth the full asking price. I'd definitely recommend waiting for a sale.

Overall, Viewfinder is a unique and memorable puzzle game that I'd happily recommend to anyone who enjoys creative puzzle-solving.

reviews.title: A Relaxing Desktop Companion for Short Breaks
reviews.text:
Desktop Golf is a fun little desktop companion that does exactly what it's trying to do.

The gameplay is simple but satisfying. The physics feel good, and every shot comes down to your own skill rather than luck.

There are 100 levels to complete. The game doesn't introduce many new mechanics, but it mixes in different obstacles throughout the campaign. They get reused quite a bit, so some holes can feel a little similar. That said, I don't think this is a game you're supposed to finish in one sitting. It's designed to sit on your desktop so you can play a few holes during a short break before getting back to whatever you were doing.

The controls work well overall but I wish there was a bit more freedom and convenience when moving the game window around the desktop.

The visuals are very simple, but they fit the concept nicely. The relaxing background music also suits the game's laid-back nature, even if it isn't particularly memorable.

It took me a few hours to complete all 100 holes. You can always return to earn three stars on every level or just play a few random courses when you need a quick break, but I personally felt satisfied after finishing everything.

Performance was flawless throughout my playtime.

Overall, if you're looking for a cheap, relaxing desktop game that you can enjoy in short sessions between work or other tasks, Desktop Golf is an easy recommendation.

reviews.title: A Charming Platformer That Never Runs Out of Ideas
reviews.text:
Grapple Dog is a fantastic precision platformer with very enjoyable movement that feels smooth and responsive throughout most of the game.

The grappling hook is the star of the game. Building momentum and flying through levels feels incredibly rewarding. However, the general movement can occasionally make precise platforming a bit awkward in certain situations, which is separate from the momentum gained through the grappling hook itself.

The level design is excellent throughout. Every chapter introduces new themes and mechanics at a steady pace, so the game always feels fresh. There's also plenty of optional content, including collectibles, time trials, races, gem and combat challenges, giving completionists a lot to do.

The difficulty is fair. Finishing the main game isn't overly demanding, while 100% completion offers a satisfying challenge. The checkpoint system works well in the main levels, but in time trials checkpoints are replaced with health pickups. In some levels, you're forced past these pickups without the ability to backtrack, leaving you stuck with low health, which can be a bit frustrating.

The colorful pixel art looks great, animations are smooth, and the soundtrack is catchy, upbeat, and perfectly fits the game's atmosphere.

The game is well paced, never feels too long, and I didn't experience any technical issues during my playthrough.

Overall, Grapple Dog is a polished, creative, and consistently fun platformer that I would happily recommend to anyone who enjoys fast-paced 2D platformers.

reviews.title: A Cozy and Satisfying Cleaning Experience
reviews.text:
Cozy Cleaner is a relaxing and satisfying cleaning game that's easy to just sit back and enjoy.

The cleaning itself feels pretty nice. A couple of new tools are introduced early on, and you can upgrade them throughout the game to make them faster. Most areas have different looks and layouts, although the actual gameplay remains mostly the same each time.

The unique levels that appear between the regular ones were a nice addition and helped break up the repetition. That said, the game did start to feel a little repetitive towards the end.

The visuals are quite simple, but they work well for creating the cozy atmosphere the game is going for. The relaxing soundtrack also fits really well and is nice to have playing in the background.

My main issue is the amount of content. I feel like the game is a little too short for the full asking price, so I'd recommend picking it up on sale. The game does mention that more content will be added in the future, which is good to see.

I had a completely clean playthrough with no technical issues.

Overall, I'd recommend Cozy Cleaner if you're looking for a simple and relaxing game to unwind with. Just keep in mind that the gameplay can become repetitive and the current content feels a little limited.

reviews.title: A Charming Little Possession Puzzle Game
reviews.text:
Henry Halfhead is a charming and creative little puzzle game built around a really fun possession mechanic.

You can interact with and control pretty much anything around you, which leads to a lot of fun and creative situations. The puzzles make good use of this ability and there’s a decent mix throughout the game, although most of them are on the easier side. The only thing that occasionally annoyed me was trying to possess one specific item when there were a lot of objects piled together.

The visuals are fairly simple but fit the vibe of the game nicely. Henry himself is adorable, and the different areas have a good amount of variation. The character expressions also add some extra charm.

I enjoyed the humor and overall presentation. Nothing in particular stood out, but the game maintains a fun and playful tone throughout. The music and sound design complement the experience well too.

I also liked following Henry through his entire life. The way the story is presented is a little different from what you normally see in games, and I thought it worked really well alongside the gameplay. It creates a good balance between the narrative and the puzzles.

The game only took me a few hours to finish, which felt like a reasonable length for this experience. However, I think the asking price is a little too high for the amount of content. I’d recommend picking it up on sale instead.

I had a smooth experience overall without running into any notable technical issues.

A fun, quirky and creative little game with a great central mechanic. Recommended, especially if you enjoy shorter puzzle games with a lot of personality.

reviews.title: A Charming Puzzle Adventure With A Beautiful Art Style
reviews.text:
The visual style was what initially caught my attention with Inked: A Tale of Love, and thankfully the gameplay was enjoyable enough to keep me interested throughout.

The puzzles are one of the strongest parts of the game. There's a good variation between them, they're well balanced, and the environments and mechanics are incorporated nicely into the puzzles.

The gameplay generally feels good, and new mechanics are introduced at a good pace as you progress. I wasn't immediately sold on the click-to-move controls, but they felt better the more I played. Moving objects around could sometimes feel a little clunky though.

Visually, I really liked the ink-and-paper style and the world design. Each chapter has its own unique look and the environments are nicely varied.

I also enjoyed the story. It strikes a good balance between the narrative and puzzles, and I liked how the creator who is drawing everything is incorporated into the story. You get to experience his story and struggles and see how they affect the world you're playing through.

The music is nice and relaxing for the most part, while changing to fit what is happening and the atmosphere of each situation.

The game is relatively short, but I think the length is just right for this experience. I wouldn't really want it to be much longer or shorter.

I did encounter one issue in the final chapter where I spawned outside the playable area after taking a portal and got stuck. I had to restart the entire chapter, but thankfully this was the only major issue I encountered.

Overall, Inked: A Tale of Love is a charming puzzle adventure with a great visual style, varied puzzles, and a relaxing atmosphere. Recommended if you enjoy story-driven puzzle games. The price is reasonable, although I'd personally wait for a small sale.

reviews.title: A Beautiful World Worth Cleaning Up
reviews.text:
The Gunk is a fun exploration game with a satisfying cleaning mechanic and a beautiful world.

The general gameplay feels solid, with smooth and responsive movement. Exploring is rewarding thanks to optional paths that lead to extra resources, which can be used to build upgrades. The upgrades aren't anything too crazy, but they feel meaningful and progression moves at a good pace. I also liked that you can backtrack.

The scanning mechanic was more mixed for me. Since scanning unique things unlocks upgrades, I often found myself scanning everything because I didn't want to miss anything. It took me a while to realize there are icons showing whether something has already been scanned, and the short scanning range meant I still had to get fairly close to objects to check them.

Cleaning up the Gunk is mostly satisfying, especially when you see the environment transform back into something more colorful and full of life. It can get a little slow and repetitive at times, though.

The puzzles are alright and generally quite easy, but I think they have a good balance and don't take too much focus away from the story. I also liked how they use the game's mechanics and environments.

The game looks beautiful and has a great atmosphere. There is some variation between areas, although most of them naturally have a similar vibe since you're exploring the same planet. Seeing the world change as you clean it was a highlight.

The story kept me engaged throughout, although I found the characters themselves less interesting. The music, sound design, and voice acting are all good and contribute nicely to the atmosphere.

It's a little short, but the pacing is good throughout, so I didn't mind the length.

I did encounter a spot where I became completely stuck and had to reload the latest checkpoint. Luckily, it wasn't far back. Towards the end, I also experienced a huge performance drop on the large elevator, with the framerate dropping to around 10 FPS.

Overall, I really enjoyed The Gunk and would definitely recommend it.

reviews.title: A One-Note Joke That Forgets to Be a Game
reviews.text:
How to Train Your ♥♥♥♥ is a passive idle game that never really finds a reason to hold your attention.

The training loop is about as inert as it sounds. I checked in regularly early on and grabbed the right upgrades at the right times, so the pacing stayed reasonable compared to what other people described. Even with that active management, there just wasn't much happening on screen. Watching a ♥♥♥♥ lift weights and slowly bulk up sounds like it should have some charm, but it plays more like a background process than a game.

The cosmetics and hats only mattered to me for the stat bonuses attached to them. I never cared how my ♥♥♥♥ actually looked.

The Pounder Place, the punching arcade minigame, confused me at first. By the time I understood what it was doing, I'd already lost interest and stopped touching it.

The leaderboard and social features around visiting friends or comparing progress didn't pull me in either. I never touched them.

The presentation and humor was one of the few things working in its favor, but even that only carried it for a few minutes. It's mildly amusing at first, then the joke runs out of steam fast.

No bugs or crashes to report, for what that's worth.

Overall, I can't recommend How to Train Your ♥♥♥♥. It's a shallow idle game riding entirely on its premise, and once the joke wears off there's little reason to keep it open. I only played it because it came in a bundle, and I doubt I'd have looked twice otherwise. Not worth the current price. It should be cheaper, or even free.

reviews.title: A Cozy Desktop Companion That Never Quite Hatches Into Something Gripping
reviews.text:
Little Aviary is a decent idea that never quite clicked into a game I cared about.

The pitch is simple. You get a little aviary that sits on your desktop, birds hatch, fly around, and the whole thing is meant to just live in the background while you do other things. It asks a bit more of you at the start than I expected, but once things got going it settled nicely into my second monitor without demanding much attention.

The core loop of hatching, breeding, selling, and decorating never really landed for me though. I bred birds because quests told me to, not because I wanted to. Same with decorating, that was purely for achievements. Nothing about it felt engaging, but it wasn't repetitive either. It just sat there, neutral.

The zoom and reposition system was more annoying than I expected. Once you've placed a few decorations, moving or resizing the window gets fiddly and things start getting in the way. On the plus side, watching the birds actually behave was one of the better parts.

Visually the game is very nice, and the music is a genuine vibe to have running in the background. The egg hatching sound effect stuck out in a bad way though, it just didn't fit the rest of the game's tone at all.

I didn't hit any actual bugs, but the tutorial section rubbed me the wrong way for reasons I can't fully pin down, and the transitions between areas felt a bit off too. Small things, but they added up.

For the price, this is a cheap game and it delivers reasonable value for what it costs.

I'd still recommend Little Aviary, mainly because it's inexpensive and the concept of a chill desktop companion is a nice one. Just go in expecting some rough edges. It's best suited for people who want ambient background music and cute bird animations more than anyone looking for a deep or gripping idle loop.

reviews.title: A Tense and Addictive Slot Machine Roguelike
reviews.text:
Cloverpit is a slot machine roguelike that had me hooked from the start. The core loop of spinning, weighing risk against reward, and deciding when to push your luck versus bank your gains is genuinely tense and satisfying. The only downside is that early runs can go sideways fast if the shop doesn't offer good starting items and the machine gives you a string of dry spins, sometimes ending a run before it really begins.

The progression system is excellent. There are a huge number of items to unlock, and most of them keep opening up naturally as you play, as long as you're not leaning on the same build every time. Working toward the ending and eventually beating the game gives every run a sense of purpose beyond just that session's score.

Build variety is one of the strongest parts of the game. What you get early on nudges you toward certain strategies, but you're never locked in, and pivoting mid run is part of the fun. I settled into a few reliable go to builds that almost guaranteed a win, but experimenting with different combinations stayed enjoyable throughout.

Visually the game nails its vibe. Outside of the ending you're mostly stuck in one small room, but the atmosphere carries it. The art style fits perfectly, and the music is a genuine highlight. Sound design across the board pulls you in and makes you want to keep spinning.

Run length is flexible. A straightforward push to the ending can be quick, but if you're chasing bigger totals or trying to hit specific requirements there's no natural stopping point, so runs can stretch out depending on how greedy you get.

Replayability holds up well thanks to the modifier cards that unlock later, each playable on normal and then hard difficulty. This adds a lot of longevity once the base unlocks start running dry.

I didn't run into any bugs or technical issues during my playthrough.

Overall I'd recommend Cloverpit without hesitation. It scratches the gambling itch in a way that's actually fun and costs you nothing beyond the price of admission, which beats the alternative of losing real money. And at 13 Euros for the base game plus DLC, what you get as a whole is still a great price, even with some grumbling that the DLC should have been a free update instead.
